modules.title: 1. From Python programs to a maintainable Django application
modules.description: Start only after Common Foundation. Required shared concepts include Python contracts/collections/environments, SQL, Git, tests, HTTP and privacy. These are prerequisites, not lessons repeated here. Use Python, Django 5.2, PostgreSQL 18 and server-rendered templates; add DRF for JSON endpoints. Keep tests and secure defaults from the first slice.

lessons.title: Trace a request through a Django application
objectives: Trace URL resolution, view execution, template rendering and response generation.
Separate configuration and application code and explain development-server limits.

topics.title: Application structure
details: Project versus app; settings, URL configuration and request/response objects.
WSGI/ASGI entry points at a conceptual level; a development server is not a production deployment.

topics.title: Boundaries
details: View responsibilities versus pure business functions.
Environment-specific configuration, explicit errors and secret-free startup instructions.

video.locator: Week 3: Django; watch the official lecture, then trace its URL/view/template examples.

reading.locator: Writing your first Django app, part 1: Creating a project; Creating the Polls app; Write your first view. https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/intro/tutorial01/

assignment.title: Build an original synthetic shop service skeleton
instructions: Create health and catalogue-summary routes using a new fictional shop name, not the tutorial poll domain.
Move summary calculation into a pure function and document one complete request trace.
Read configuration from an explicit local setup and add one passing and one invalid-route test.
deliverables: Runnable application skeleton with pinned direct dependencies
acceptanceCriteria: A clean local environment can start the application using documented commands.
Health returns the documented status/body; an unknown route returns 404.
No credentials or machine-specific absolute paths are committed.
The explanation identifies where routing, domain work and rendering occur.

reviewPrompts: What work should not be done in a view?
What changes when replacing the development server?
Which configuration belongs outside source control?

lessons.title: Model application state and evolve its schema
objectives: Translate domain rules into relationships and database constraints.
Create and safely apply schema/data migrations against PostgreSQL.

topics.title: Operational model
details: Product, stock, order and order-line ownership; foreign keys and uniqueness.
Money represented with Decimal or integer minor units; explicit currency and immutable order-price snapshots.

topics.title: Evolution
details: Model state versus applied migrations; schema versus data migrations.
Backward-compatible changes, defaults, nullable transitions and rollback limitations.

video.locator: Week 4: SQL, Models, and Migrations.

reading.locator: Writing your first Django app, part 2: Database setup; Creating models; Activating models; Playing with the API. https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/intro/tutorial02/

assignment.title: Create a constrained shop schema
instructions: Design and migrate a schema for 100 synthetic products and a small set of orders.
Add database constraints for unique product codes, nonnegative stock and positive line quantities.
Introduce a new shipping-rule field in a second migration and describe a compatible release order.
acceptanceCriteria: Invalid rows fail through the database as well as through form validation.
A fresh database and an upgraded database produce equivalent expected schemas and fixtures.
Changing a catalogue price does not silently change an existing order's price snapshot.
The release note describes what is reversible and what needs data recovery.

reviewPrompts: Why can an application check fail to protect an invariant?
Why store an order's price snapshot?
When is reversing a migration unsafe?

lessons.title: Build server-rendered forms with accessible feedback
objectives: Implement a POST/redirect/GET form flow with server-side validation.
Provide semantic controls, labels and comprehensible success/error states.

topics.title: Browser/server contract
details: Templates, escaping, URL names, form binding and validation.
CSRF protection, POST/redirect/GET and server-calculated values.

topics.title: Usable interfaces
details: Labels, field grouping, error summaries and keyboard navigation.
Minimal CSS layouts, empty states and avoiding unnecessary personal data.

video.locator: Week 0: HTML and CSS; apply the semantic form/layout concepts to the existing Django app.

reading.locator: Chapter 8: Prettification: Layout and Styling, and What to Test About It; Chapter 15: A Simple Form.

assignment.title: Create a catalogue and cart-editing slice
instructions: Render a catalogue and an add/update-cart form using templates, not a frontend framework.
Reject zero, negative, noninteger and out-of-range quantities on the server.
Add labelled fields, persistent validation errors and keyboard-only navigation instructions.
deliverables: Keyboard walkthrough and screenshots containing only synthetic data
acceptanceCriteria: Each control has an accessible name and all actions can be reached by keyboard.
Refreshing after a successful POST does not repeat the form submission.
Invalid input preserves the user's safe values and exposes a specific error.
Client-submitted totals never determine the server price.

reviewPrompts: What does POST/redirect/GET solve and not solve?
Why is client-side validation insufficient?
What distinguishes a visible label from a placeholder?

modules.title: 2. Contracts, permissions and transaction-safe APIs
modules.description: Extend the working application with explicit JSON contracts and transaction correctness. Foundation SQL/HTTP are assumed; the new work is validation, ownership, real concurrent database sessions and replay-safe side effects.

lessons.title: Design and implement a small versioned JSON contract
objectives: Describe request, response, validation and error shapes before implementation.
Implement a DRF endpoint with predictable pagination and compatibility tests.

topics.title: Contract design
details: Resources versus commands; methods, status codes, pagination and stable ordering.
OpenAPI 3.1.1 schemas, required/optional fields and additive versus breaking changes.

topics.title: Implementation boundaries
details: DRF serializers, read-only fields and consistent error responses.
Explicit supported filters and bounded page sizes; unknown input policy.

video.locator: Week 5: JavaScript; the browser/API interaction examples motivate the server contract. DRF specifics are in the supplementary tutorial.

reading.locator: Appendix E: Building a REST API: JSON, Ajax, and Mocking with JavaScript.

assignment.title: Specify catalogue and order-draft endpoints
instructions: Write an original OpenAPI contract for product listing, product detail and order-draft creation.
Implement the endpoints with bounded pagination and server-owned price fields.
Write request/response tests and add one backward-compatible optional response field.
deliverables: Positive, validation, pagination and compatibility tests
acceptanceCriteria: The contract documents every implemented response status and required field.
Repeated paginated reads have deterministic ordering on unchanged fixtures.
Malformed quantities, excessive page sizes and unknown product IDs have documented outcomes.
A client using the original response fields still passes after the additive change.

reviewPrompts: When is a new response field still a breaking change?
Why must pagination specify ordering?
Which fields must never be writable by the client?

lessons.title: Enforce customer, staff and object ownership boundaries
objectives: Distinguish authentication, role checks and object-level authorization.
Apply ownership rules to detail, list and mutation paths consistently.

topics.title: Identity and sessions
details: Framework-provided users, password handling, sessions, login/logout and CSRF.
Secure cookie settings; authorization failures without leaking sensitive records.

topics.title: Access enforcement
details: Customer-owned orders and explicitly scoped staff capabilities.
Queryset filtering, create-time ownership assignment, object checks and direct-ID access.

video.locator: Week 4: SQL, Models, and Migrations; revisit its Django user/application-data examples. Current authorization semantics are in the manual and DRF permissions guide.

reading.locator: Using the Django authentication system: User objects; Permissions and Authorization; Authentication in web requests. https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/topics/auth/default/

assignment.title: Build and test an ownership matrix
instructions: Create two customers, one staff user and synthetic orders belonging to each customer.
Define permissions for listing, viewing and changing an order before implementing them.
Test anonymous, owner, other-customer and staff requests for each operation.
deliverables: At least twelve role/operation test cases
acceptanceCriteria: Other-customer orders are absent from lists and inaccessible by direct identifiers.
Submitted owner IDs cannot transfer ownership.
Staff power is explicitly granted rather than inferred from knowing an identifier.
Passwords are handled by Django, not by custom hashing or plaintext storage.

questions.prompt: A user is logged in and an order identifier exists. What additional fact must be checked before returning that order?
questions.answer: Whether this user has permission to access this specific order, such as ownership or an explicitly granted staff capability.
questions.explanation: Authentication establishes who is calling; it does not establish access to every object.

reviewPrompts: Why are list and detail permissions separate concerns?
Where should ownership be assigned during creation?
What is unsafe about relying on a hidden UI button?

lessons.title: Prevent overselling with real PostgreSQL transactions
objectives: Explain a lost-update or check-then-act race using an interleaving.
Implement and verify a stock reservation invariant under concurrent sessions.

topics.title: Transaction semantics
details: Read Committed, row locks, atomic updates, constraints and rollback.
Consistent lock ordering, deadlock handling and bounded retry of a whole transaction.

topics.title: Django integration
details: transaction.atomic and select_for_update; avoid network calls while holding stock locks.
TransactionTestCase or an external concurrent-session harness; SQLite is not a substitute.

video.locator: Lecture #16: Concurrency Control Theory, 30 October 2024; optional follow-up Lecture #19: Multi-Version Concurrency Control.

reading.locator: 13.2 Transaction Isolation, especially Read Committed; 13.3 Explicit Locking, especially Row-Level Locks and Deadlocks.

assignment.title: Race two purchasers for scarce stock
instructions: Start with seven units and two independent requests for five units each.
Write down a failing naive interleaving, then implement a transaction-safe reservation.
Use separate PostgreSQL connections and a synchronization barrier; repeat the scenario twenty times and inject a failure before commit.
deliverables: Concurrent-session test harness and raw run output
acceptanceCriteria: At most one five-unit reservation succeeds from seven available units.
Stock never becomes negative and successful reservations reconcile to stock movement.
The injected pre-commit failure leaves neither an order nor consumed stock.
Tests demonstrate separate connections and actual overlapping execution, not two sequential calls.

questions.prompt: Seven units exist. Two concurrent orders each require five units and partial fulfillment is disallowed. What is the maximum number of successful orders?
questions.explanation: Two successful orders would require ten units; the invariant permits only one complete reservation.

reviewPrompts: Why is checking stock before the transaction insufficient?
What must be retried after a serialization/deadlock failure?
Why can a Django TestCase hide missing transaction boundaries?

lessons.title: Make simulated payment callbacks replay-safe
objectives: Define idempotency scope, key lifetime and conflicting-replay behaviour.
Apply a business transition once despite repeated or concurrent delivery.

topics.title: Replay semantics
details: Request/event IDs, payload fingerprints, unique constraints and recorded results.
Same-key/same-payload replay versus same-key/different-payload conflict.

topics.title: Effects and recovery
details: Atomic recording of the event and its local state change.
Simulated external effects; deduplication is not a guarantee of exactly-once network delivery.

video.locator: Lecture #22: Introduction to Distributed Databases, 20 November 2024; use its distributed-failure context, then implement application-level idempotency from the readings.

reading.locator: Chapter 6: Unit of Work Pattern; Chapter 10: Commands and Command Handler.

assignment.title: Process one simulated payment event many times
instructions: Implement a local callback simulator with event ID, order ID and an integer minor-unit amount.
Store deduplication information and the order-state change in one database transaction.
Exercise twenty repeated calls, two concurrent calls and a changed payload reusing the same ID.
acceptanceCriteria: Repeated identical delivery causes one successful payment-state transition.
Conflicting payload reuse is rejected with the documented error and no new effect.
A crash before commit permits a safe retry; a replay after commit returns a consistent outcome.
The project handles no real card data, bank credentials or financial transfers.

reviewPrompts: What scope makes an idempotency key meaningful?
Why is a cache-only deduplication record risky?
Which guarantee remains impossible across an uncontrolled external service?

modules.title: 3. Domain architecture and distributed failure
modules.description: Keep a modular monolith unless a real requirement justifies distribution. Introduce explicit business services, workflows, durable background work and bounded failure handling without making Kubernetes, Kafka or microservices compulsory.

lessons.title: Separate business policy from transport and storage
objectives: Express one use case as a service with explicit inputs and outputs.
Explain the benefit and cost of an abstraction using a concrete change scenario.

topics.title: Domain boundaries
details: Entities, value objects, invariants and service-layer use cases.
Dependency direction, pure policy functions and explicit persistence boundaries.

topics.title: Pragmatic architecture
details: Repository/unit-of-work concepts versus Django's existing abstractions.
An architecture decision record and avoiding layers that do not solve a demonstrated problem.

video.locator: Week 3: Django; revisit the request/view boundaries, then compare them with the service-layer reading.

reading.locator: Chapter 1: Domain Modeling; Chapter 4: Our First Use Case: Flask API and Service Layer; Appendix D: Repository and Unit of Work Patterns with Django.

assignment.title: Extract an explainable checkout service
instructions: Move checkout policy out of views without changing the public API.
Make one policy replaceable in a test, such as shipping eligibility, while retaining real database integration tests.
Write a short decision record comparing direct ORM use with a repository abstraction.
deliverables: Decision record with one rejected alternative
acceptanceCriteria: Existing contract and reservation tests still pass unchanged.
Policy tests can execute without HTTP routing.
The design names a concrete benefit and cost of each introduced abstraction.
No second web framework or distributed deployment is added merely to match the book.

reviewPrompts: What is a use case rather than a CRUD method?
When is the Django ORM enough?
What evidence would justify extracting a service?

lessons.title: Represent returns and exchanges as guarded state transitions
objectives: Specify permitted transitions and quantity/accounting invariants.
Reject illegal, stale and unauthorized transitions explicitly.

topics.title: Workflow policy
details: Requested, approved, received and resolved states; rejection and cancellation policy.
Partial returns, cumulative eligible quantities, version checks and append-only audit events.

topics.title: Atomic changes
details: Exchange-stock reservation and simulated-credit deduplication.
A standalone application with imported fixtures rather than an implicit dependency on the storefront.

video.locator: Week 4: SQL, Models, and Migrations; apply relationship modelling to the workflow described in the book and assignment.

reading.locator: Chapter 7: Aggregates and Consistency Boundaries; Chapter 10: Commands and Command Handler.

assignment.title: Build a standalone partial-return state machine
instructions: Define a small return policy for synthetic fulfilled orders and list all permitted transitions.
Implement three fulfilled units with multiple partial-return attempts and separate customer/staff commands.
Atomically reserve replacement stock only when an exchange transition succeeds.
acceptanceCriteria: Cumulative accepted return quantities never exceed eligible fulfilled quantities.
Every undefined transition fails explicitly without changing state.
A failed exchange leaves stock and simulated credits unchanged.
The workflow can run from its own fixtures without the storefront database.

reviewPrompts: Why is a status field alone not a state machine?
Where should cumulative return eligibility be enforced?
What makes an audit event different from the current state?

lessons.title: Use an outbox and retryable worker for durable work
objectives: Close the commit-then-publish gap with a durable work record.
Handle crashes and repeated delivery with bounded retries and compensating actions.

topics.title: Durability and delivery
details: Outbox row and business change in one transaction; polling worker and claim/lease policy.
At-least-once processing, idempotent handlers, retry scheduling and manual-recovery state.

topics.title: Orchestration
details: Inventory/order/simulated-payment steps with explicit progress records.
Compensation versus database rollback; reconciliation when an external outcome is unknown.

video.locator: Lecture #22: Introduction to Distributed Databases; focus on the problem of coordinating state across failures, not on building a distributed database.

reading.locator: Chapter 8: Events and the Message Bus; Chapter 11: Event-Driven Architecture: Using Events to Integrate Microservices.

assignment.title: Create a crash-recoverable local order worker
instructions: Write a durable order-work record in the same transaction as the order.
Run a separate local worker process with bounded retries and persisted progress; a PostgreSQL-backed queue is sufficient.
Inject crashes before commit, after commit/before dispatch and after a simulated effect/before acknowledgement.
Document a compensation and reconciliation policy without claiming global exactly-once execution.
deliverables: Recovery tests and a manual-recovery command
acceptanceCriteria: Every committed order requiring work has a durable work record.
Each injected crash can be followed by a restart that reaches a consistent terminal or explicitly recoverable state.
Retries do not duplicate stock consumption or simulated payment effects.
Permanently failing work stops automatic retries at a configured bound and is visible for investigation.

reviewPrompts: Why is on_commit alone not durable delivery?
Which side effects can be compensated rather than rolled back?
How do you handle a timeout with an unknown external result?

lessons.title: Budget timeouts, retries, caching and overload
objectives: Allocate a request deadline across dependencies and retries.
Define cache consistency and overload behaviour without corrupting business state.

topics.title: Bounded resource use
details: Connection timeouts, total deadlines, retry budgets, exponential backoff and jitter.
Bounded queues, concurrency limits and deliberate failure responses rather than unbounded waiting.

topics.title: Consistency trade-offs
details: Cache keys, invalidation, stale reads and tenant/user boundaries.
Never authorize from an unsafe shared cache or promise stock availability from stale catalogue data.

video.locator: Week 8: Scalability and Security; caching/load-distribution ideas, extended by the SRE overload chapters.

reading.locator: Chapter 21: Handling Overload; Chapter 22: Addressing Cascading Failures.

assignment.title: Bound a slow dependency and a product cache
instructions: Create a local fake shipping-rate dependency with configurable delay and failure.
Choose a total request budget, retry bound and queue/concurrency limit; state them before measuring.
Cache a safe catalogue representation and prove that checkout still reads authoritative stock/prices.
deliverables: Local failure simulator and cache policy
acceptanceCriteria: The test asserts a documented deadline tolerance, not merely that a request eventually returns.
A permanently failing dependency triggers no more than the configured retry count.
Cache entries cannot leak one customer's or tenant's data to another.
Stale catalogue data cannot authorize an overselling checkout.

reviewPrompts: Why can retries make an outage worse?
What must a cache key include?
Which data can safely be stale and which cannot?

assignment.title: Prove boundaries for two fictional sellers
instructions: Draw the trust boundaries for two sellers, two customers and staff.
Define at least eight cross-boundary misuse cases covering detail/list/create/update/export/worker/search/cache paths.
Implement a representative seller-scoped read and write and test the trusted tenant context.

Detail, list and creation paths enforce the same ownership policy.
Background work contains and validates the intended tenant context.

Debug details and secrets are absent from deployed error responses.

reviewPrompts: Why is input validation not a replacement for output encoding?

limitations: This is additional SDE learning after Common Foundation, not a substitute for it and not a union of Data/Quant/AI advanced curricula. Module prerequisites reference only modules in this file. Shared canonicalConceptTags identify prior concepts; an overlapping tag is not proof that an advanced lesson has already been completed.

All 29 lessons, all assignments and all five reconstruction/build evidence packages start incomplete. No progress, completion date, measured outcome, recovered repository, employment guarantee or production-readiness claim is initialized.

Estimated minutes include selective reading/video review and the bounded lesson assignment, not full independent implementation of all five portfolio projects. Reused lectures need not be watched in full every time. Actual effort varies with prior proficiency and debugging.

Lessons sde-l25-fullstack and sde-l26-platform are optional branches. Lessons sde-l27-lexical-search and sde-l28-rerank-evaluation are specialist work for the B search project. Do not make all four optional-depth lessons a universal backend completion gate.

Primary stack is Python, Django 5.2, PostgreSQL 18, DRF for JSON APIs, server-rendered templates, Django tests and optional Playwright browser tests. Cosmos/TDD examples sometimes use Flask, SQLAlchemy, Selenium or Ansible; translate principles rather than adding every tool. Kubernetes and microservices are not prerequisites.

Select and pin mutually compatible supported Python, Django, DRF, database-driver and optional model-library versions at implementation time. The current optional Azure guide specifies Python 3.14 or higher; older lecture environments are not authoritative installation recipes.

CS50 recordings and MIT security lectures are older but useful for durable concepts. Current official manuals and ASVS accompany them. Video page/title/locator availability was verified through public HTTP, not through full playback, regional accessibility or signed-in account testing. Videos are link/embed-only; none were downloaded.
No PDFs were downloaded. PostgreSQL and OWASP PDF URLs were checked with HEAD only; their actual bytes, integrity, accessibility and retained notices must be checked by implementation before hosting.

PostgreSQL documentation and OWASP ASVS are positively licensed hosting candidates with the recorded notice/share-alike conditions. Django repository documentation is BSD-licensed, but this does not grant rights to unrelated site assets or logos.

TDD with Python has a verified book-specific CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 US license; SWE at Google and the SRE book have CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. They remain link-only here until noncommercial deployment and redistribution conditions are confirmed. Do not create or distribute adapted NC-ND book chapters.

Cosmic Python licensing is unversioned and inconsistent between its author landing page and repository license file. Its authorized free reading is useful, but hosting permission is not asserted. The Stanford IR book also remains link-only; free PDF availability is not redistribution permission.

Some web extractors returned only page navigation or individual chapter fragments. Relevant HTML headings/TOCs were checked by read-only public HTTP and, where necessary, official raw repository sources. MIT 6.824 and 6.033 candidate URLs were not reliably retrievable and were not included; verified CMU recordings were used instead.

Hosted GitHub runs, Azure provisioning, container software entitlement and model hardware requirements may involve accounts, quotas, cost or licensing restrictions. Core exercises have local alternatives. No repository, account, cloud resource or signed-in browser tab was changed by this curation.

Neural retrieval uses optional pretrained components as application dependencies, not a model-training curriculum. The exact chosen model's license/revision and dataset rights must be checked before later download. Hardware/licensing blocks leave that milestone incomplete, never replaced with invented scores.

The A projects are independent reconstruction exercises for user-reported college work whose original files were lost. The B projects remain future builds. Use only synthetic/publicly lawful data; no employer/client code, reports, credentials, identities or private assets.
